title: The $3,100 Credit Card Balance That Takes 15 Years to Pay Off – The 21% Math
title_card: What does 21% interest really cost you?
description: The typical American who carries a credit card balance owes about $3,100. At today's average rate of 21%, paying only the minimum takes 15 years and costs more in interest than the balance itself. We walk through the real Federal Reserve data on card rates – now near a 30-year record – and the simple math of minimum payments, the interest-only trap and what paying a bit more changes. No advice, just the numbers.
sources: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.19 Consumer Credit, Terms of Credit: commercial bank interest rate on credit card plans, all accounts and accounts assessed interest, quarterly 1994 Q4–2026 Q3 (yearly averages computed; August 2026: 21.19% all accounts, 22.36% accounts assessed interest)
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, G.19 Consumer Credit: revolving consumer credit outstanding, not seasonally adjusted, $1,315.2 billion (August 2026)

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 'Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025' (Survey of Consumer Finances, October 2026): 44.7% of families carry a credit card balance; conditional median balance $3,100; 55.8% do not carry a balance

Illustrative calculations: interest at 21.19% a year added monthly (1/12 per month); example minimum payment of 1% of the balance plus that month's interest, at least $25 (card terms vary – check your own statement)

beats.say: Three thousand one hundred dollars. That's what the typical American who carries a credit card balance owes. Not a disaster. A couple of bad months.

show.caption: median card balance, families who carry one, 2025

beats.say: Now pay only the minimum, every month, and never use the card again. How long until it's gone?
Fifteen years. And by the end you've paid about four thousand four hundred dollars in interest – more than the balance itself.
Today: the real numbers behind credit card interest, the trap built into the minimum payment, and the one balance where paying a hundred dollars a month never ends.
Quick note: this is general information, not financial advice.

show.text: Card terms vary. *Check your own statement.*
show.source: Every payoff in this video is an example calculation

beats.say: First, the rate. Here's the average interest rate on credit card accounts at US banks, from the Federal Reserve, over thirty years.

show.heading: Average US credit card interest rate
show.sub: Commercial banks, all accounts, yearly average 1995–2025 · Federal Reserve G.19

beats.say: In the late nineties: around sixteen percent.
Then it drifted down for almost twenty years. In 2014, the average was under twelve percent.
Then the Fed raised interest rates fast in 2022 and 2023 to fight inflation – and card rates follow right behind.
In 2024, the yearly average hit twenty-one point six percent. The highest in this whole thirty-year series.
And it hasn't come down much. In August 2026: twenty-one point one nine percent across all accounts.

show.caption: average card rate, all accounts, Aug 2026

beats.say: For people who actually pay interest – who carry a balance – it's even higher: twenty-two point three six percent.

What does that jump mean for you? On the same three thousand one hundred dollar balance, a year of interest at the 2014 rate was about three hundred and seventy dollars. At today's rate it's about six hundred and fifty-seven. Same debt, almost twice the cost – and you didn't do anything differently.
And Americans owe about one point three trillion dollars in revolving credit – mostly credit cards.
So how does twenty-one percent actually hit your balance? It's charged a little every month: twenty-one point one nine divided by twelve.

show.source: Most cards actually charge a daily rate – the result is about the same

beats.say: On three thousand one hundred dollars, that's about fifty-five dollars of interest in the first month alone.
Over a full year, if the balance just sat there, that's about six hundred and fifty-seven dollars. For nothing new. Just for keeping the old stuff.
Here's the part almost nobody knows. If you pay your full statement balance by the due date, most cards charge you nothing at all. That's called the grace period.
So the same plastic card is two completely different products. Paid in full, it's free. Carried over, it's one of the most expensive loans you can get.
And according to the Fed, about fifty-six percent of families never carry a balance. They use exactly the same cards – and pay no interest.
Now the minimum payment. Card terms vary, but a common formula is: one percent of the balance, plus that month's interest, and at least twenty-five dollars.
On three thousand one hundred dollars, your first minimum is about eighty-six dollars. Sounds fine. But fifty-five of those dollars are interest. Only thirty-one actually pay down what you owe.
And here's the trap. As the balance shrinks, the minimum shrinks with it. The bank keeps asking for less – so it takes longer and longer.

show.heading: Paying off $3,100 at 21.19%
show.sub: Balance left, by year · minimum = 1% + interest, at least $25 · example

beats.say: The red line is minimum payments only. The gold one we'll come back to. After one year, you still owe about two thousand seven hundred.
After five years, you've paid almost three thousand nine hundred dollars – more than you ever borrowed – and you still owe about seventeen hundred.
The line only reaches zero after fifteen years.
Total interest: about four thousand four hundred dollars. A three-thousand-dollar balance turned into a seventy-five-hundred-dollar bill.
Now look at the gold line. Same balance, same rate. The only change is a fixed payment.

show.heading: Paying off $3,100 at 21.19%
show.sub: Balance left, by year · minimum = 1% + interest, at least $25 · example

beats.say: A hundred dollars a month – just fourteen dollars more than the first minimum – and the gold line hits zero in under four years.
Two hundred dollars a month, and it's gone in nineteen months.
Here's what that does to the interest.
Minimum only: about four thousand four hundred dollars in interest.
A hundred a month: about fourteen hundred. You save three thousand dollars just by not letting the payment shrink.
Two hundred a month: about five hundred and fifty. Three hundred a month: about three hundred and fifty.
The most important number on your statement isn't the minimum. It's the amount you choose. Pick a fixed number and keep paying it, even when the minimum drops.

show.text: Pay a *fixed* amount – not a shrinking minimum.
show.source: How it works – check your own card's terms

beats.say: If this already changed how you look at your card statement, leave a like – it really helps the channel.
Now the scariest number in this video. At twenty-one point one nine percent, a hundred dollars a month only covers the interest on about five thousand six hundred and sixty dollars.

show.caption: where $100 a month only covers the interest

beats.say: Owe more than that, and a hundred-dollar payment doesn't even pay the interest. The balance grows while you're paying.
Take six thousand dollars, and pay a hundred dollars every single month.

show.heading: $6,000 at 21.19%, paying $100 a month
show.sub: Balance left, by year · illustrative calculation

beats.say: After one year, you've paid twelve hundred dollars – and you owe more than when you started.
After five years: six thousand dollars paid. Balance: about sixty-six hundred.
After ten years: twelve thousand dollars paid. Twice the original debt. And the balance is now about eight thousand four hundred.
Ten years of payments, and you're deeper in than on day one. That's compounding working against you – the same force that makes savings grow, pointed the other way.
The way out is simple math: the payment has to be bigger than the interest. Here that means more than about a hundred and six dollars a month just to start shrinking it.
Here's a way of seeing card debt that changes how it feels. Every dollar of a twenty-one percent balance you pay off saves you twenty-one cents of interest a year.

show.source: Simple math, not an investment recommendation

beats.say: That's a sure thing. For comparison, look back at the Fed's own savings data: the typical family has about eight thousand two hundred dollars in checking and savings – and a typical savings account pays far less than twenty-one percent.

So a family that holds cash at a low rate and carries a card balance at twenty-one percent at the same time is paying the difference every month. Many families keep some cash for emergencies anyway, and for good reason – but it helps to see the gap.
Back to the three thousand one hundred dollars. Interest at the minimum: about four thousand four hundred. That money doesn't buy anything. It's the price of time.

show.caption: interest paid on $3,100, minimum payments only

beats.say: So how do people actually get out? There are two well-known methods, and the math of both is simple.

show.text: Pay more than the interest. *Then choose an order.*

beats.say: Method one: the avalanche. You pay the minimum on every card, and put every extra dollar on the card with the highest rate. Mathematically, that saves the most interest.

Method two: the snowball. You put the extra dollars on the smallest balance first. It costs a bit more interest, but you see a card hit zero sooner – and for many people, that quick win keeps them going.
Both only work if one thing is true: the total you pay each month stays the same as the balances fall. When one card is paid off, its payment rolls onto the next.

show.caption: a paid-off card's payment rolls to the next

beats.say: And the cheapest debt is the one that never starts. Every purchase paid in full by the due date costs zero interest – that's what the majority of card users already do.
So, what does twenty-one percent really cost you? Three things.
One: card rates are near a thirty-year record. About twenty-one percent on average – and over twenty-two for people who carry a balance.

Two: the minimum payment is designed to shrink. Pay only the minimum on three thousand one hundred dollars, and it takes fifteen years and about four thousand four hundred in interest. A fixed hundred dollars a month cuts that to under four years.
Three: if your payment doesn't beat the interest, the balance grows forever. At twenty-one percent, a hundred a month can't win against six thousand dollars.
If you want to understand your money with real numbers, subscribe. And pull out your last statement – the interest line is the most honest number on it.
The typical American who carries a credit card balance owes about three thousand one hundred dollars. The average card rate is now about twenty-one percent – close to a thirty-year record.

show.caption: median card balance, families who carry one

beats.say: Pay only the minimum, and it takes fifteen years to clear. You pay about four thousand four hundred dollars in interest – more than you borrowed.
Why? The minimum shrinks as the balance shrinks. Your first payment is about eighty-six dollars, and fifty-five of it is just interest.

Pay a fixed hundred dollars a month instead, and it's gone in under four years. But owe six thousand, and a hundred a month doesn't even cover the interest. After ten years of paying, you'd owe more than you started with.

beats.say: The trick is to pay a fixed amount that's bigger than the interest, and keep paying it as the balance falls. The full math, step by step, is in the video on the channel.
